name: Lost Cause of the Confederacy
summary: The Lost Cause is the post-war Southern account of the Confederacy that holds secession was a lawful exercise of state sovereignty, that slavery was not the cause of the war and was a mild institution, that the South lost only to greater numbers and resources, and that its leaders and soldiers deserve reverence. Its writers also defended white supremacy against Reconstruction, and it was carried on through memorial associations, monuments and textbook campaigns.
scope: The Lost Cause as the reference works define it (Encyclopedia of Alabama, Gale/Encyclopedia.com, New Georgia Encyclopedia, NCpedia): the interpretation of the Civil War and the Old South set out by Edward A. Pollard (The Lost Cause, 1866; The Lost Cause Regained, 1868) and carried by the United Confederate Veterans and United Daughters of the Confederacy, for example in Mildred Rutherford's Measuring Rod (1919). It does not include the Confederate government's own record, later neo-Confederate or segregationist politics, or the separate memory of the war by Union supporters.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Pollard warns that a South intent on money, display and 'the civilization of material things' would lose its literature and habits of thought, and sets higher aims above 'the coarse prosperity of dollars and cents'.

decide-locally.rationale: Loyalty to states' rights was a defining principle: Rutherford's measuring rod holds the Union a compact of sovereign states, and the reference works describe the war as defended on states' rights; the sources speak of states, not of the most local level.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Pollard calls 'miscegenation' the extremity of the disease of 'Negrophilism' and treats the prospect with disgust; the Lost Cause texts present racial separation as part of the white supremacy they defend.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Pollard condemns Lincoln's suspension of habeas corpus and the military arrests as an 'era of despotism', but gives no general rule on emergencies, so the answer is moderate.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Pollard says the war did not decide 'negro equality' and that the South would keep asserting its view of it; the reference works describe white supremacy and deference of Black people to white people as part of the belief system.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Rutherford's section VI is headed 'Coercion Was Not Constitutional' and quotes Buchanan and Seward against using force on seceding states; Pollard calls Lincoln's policy one of coercion and subjugation.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: The Lost Cause treated the Confederate dead and leaders as sacred figures, with Lee, Jackson and Davis regarded as Moses and Christ figures and Memorial Day as 'the Sabbath of the South'.

natural-rulers.rationale: The Encyclopedia of Alabama says believers took the Old South as the model for relations between Black and white people and between rich and poor white people, and Pollard's stated aim was the 'supremacy of the white race'; the sources do not argue it in terms of innate fitness to rule, so the answer is moderate.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Monuments, flags and Confederate Memorial Day were the movement's central rituals, held to be sacred and to deserve 'perpetual commemoration'; the movement's own sources give no case for removing them, but its texts concern erecting and honouring them rather than keeping them against challenge.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Pollard urged the South to cherish its distinct civilization, schools and traditions after defeat, and the UDC made transmitting the South's traditional cultural values to the next generation a primary aim; the 'nation' here is the South.

racial-franchise.rationale: In The Lost Cause Regained Pollard argues against Negro suffrage as a 'brutal mockery of republicanism' and names the supremacy of the white man as the true cause the South still has to win.

restore-past-order.rationale: The sources point both ways: Pollard urged keeping the South's distinct civilization against the 'Yankee' pursuit of money while accepting the end of slavery and the Union, and diehards rejected the 'New South', yet NCpedia says New South leaders used the Lost Cause to ease the region into change.

right-to-secede.rationale: Rutherford's first two sections state that the Constitution was a compact between sovereign states, not perpetual, and that secession was not rebellion; Pollard presents the right of secession as part of the Southern view of the Union.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Pollard contrasts the agricultural South, 'scanty in shows and luxuries' but superior in moral and sentimental elements, with the Northern commercial civilization, though he does not state the claim as a general rule about city and country.

separated-powers.rationale: Pollard describes the Southern party as studying government as a system of checks and balances, and condemns Reconstruction because the Constitution's checks and balances 'no longer operate, as they were designed'.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Rutherford's Measuring Rod, adopted by the United Confederate Veterans, has a section titled that the war was not fought to hold the slaves and tells committees to reject any book that says the South fought to hold her slaves; Pollard calls slavery an incident of sectional animosity, and the reference works list this as the core tenet.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Pollard's history treats the protective tariffs, including the 'bill of abominations' of 1828, as a Northern measure that impoverished the South to enrich the North.

missingStatements.text: Slavery in the American South treated the people it held humanely.
missingStatements.rationale: Pollard and Rutherford's textbook programme both present Southern slavery as mild and the slaveholder as kind, a defining claim of the movement that no statement in the bank captures.

quotes.text: that system of servitude in the South which was really the mildest in the world
Reject a book that speaks of the slaveholder of the South as cruel and unjust to his slaves.

missingStatements.declined: A historical claim about one country.

notes: Sources read: the four reference works, Pollard's two books (searched for secession, slavery, tariffs, suffrage, race, habeas corpus, nullification, monuments themes), Rutherford's full Measuring Rod. Jefferson Davis, Alexander Stephens and Jubal Early were downloaded but not used: the defining sources name Davis and Early only as heroes or memory-makers, not as texts of the movement. Nothing found on economics, ecology, technology, religion in law, gender roles in law, foreign policy or the economy beyond tariffs; the movement is a memory and race-and-region politics, so most themes are null.
